question: COM (2026) 520 final1 acknowledges that islands are burdened with disproportionate ‘insularity costs’, particularly in the transport and housing sectors and as regards access to essential services. The report also highlighted how the ETS and the FuelEU Maritime and Alternative Fuel Infrastructure Regulations provide for exemptions and adjustments for island territories.

However, for many French and European islands, maritime connections are not a luxury, but a vital necessity for their residents, businesses, supply arrangements, health systems and territorial continuity. 1.
Can the Commission say whether it intends to prolong, extend or make permanent the exemptions under the ETS and the FuelEU Maritime Regulation that are applicable to islands?
Can it guarantee that the decarbonisation of maritime transport will not result in an increase in the cost of living for island residents?
Does the Commission intend to explicitly recognise territorial continuity as a priority criterion in any future revision of the texts mentioned above?

Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions on the EU strategy for islands, COM (2026) 520 final, Brussels, 10 June 2026 (https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/policy/themes/islands/COM_2026_520_1_EN_ACT_part1_v6.pdf) . 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.11.2026) The Commission recognises the importance to address potential issues and challenges that affect European islands and their residents, and, therefore, developed the first ever EU strategy for islands setting out a coordinated approach to support EU islands and unlock their long-term development potential.

It acknowledges that the particular circumstances facing certain islands necessitate a more gradual transition to decarbonisation. The concepts of safeguarding accessibility and efficient connectivity by maritime transport are already incorporated both in the current Emissions Trading System (ETS) and FuelEU Maritime texts.

The EU strategy for islands explicitly states that potential issues that affect the competitiveness, connectivity and cost of living of European islands will be considered as part of the reviews of the ETS and FuelEU Maritime.

In line with this approach, the Commission’s proposal for the review of the ETS that was adopted in July 2026 proposes to extend the duration of the derogation applicable for small islands until 31 December 2035 from the current 2030. ETS revenues are also available to support islands.

Member States can use their ETS revenues for climate and energy investments, including port infrastructure and maritime decarbonisation. A dedicated new EU mechanism that is proposed under the ETS review will provide companies with free ETS allowances for the uptake of sustainable fuels and clean propulsion technologies, with a bonus for those used on voyages involving islands.
